title: Gallstones: deciding when treatment is needed
intro: Gallstones are solid deposits in the gallbladder or bile ducts. Many cause no symptoms, while an obstructing stone can cause intense upper abdominal pain and sometimes infection or pancreatitis.

sections.heading: Understanding the problem
paragraphs: Typical biliary pain is strong and sustained, often in the upper right abdomen or center and sometimes radiating to the back. Bloating alone does not prove stones are responsible.

sections.heading: Assessment and tests
paragraphs: Ultrasound and blood tests help assess stones, inflammation and bile drainage. Report fever, jaundice and previous attacks; a stone found incidentally may be unrelated to another digestive complaint. Bring your medicine list and previous results; ask which findings would change the plan.

sections.heading: Treatment choices
paragraphs: Symptom-free gallbladder stones usually need observation, with selected exceptions. Recurrent attacks may lead to discussion of gallbladder removal; bile-duct stones may require endoscopic clearance. Agree how benefit and adverse effects will be checked before changing treatment.

sections.heading: Everyday care
paragraphs: Record attacks and foods that seem to trigger discomfort. Choose tolerable balanced meals while awaiting advice; drastic fasting, crash diets and commercial gallbladder flushes are not reliable cures. Choose a routine you can maintain, and discuss barriers such as cost, work or language.

sections.heading: Follow-up and warning signs
paragraphs: Severe persistent abdominal pain, fever, yellow eyes, dark urine, pale stools or repeated vomiting need urgent medical assessment. Do not wait for a scheduled operation if these appear.

examples.title: A practical example
examples.text: In this hypothetical example, Mira has stones found during an unrelated scan but no biliary symptoms. She asks why monitoring is preferable to automatic surgery.

examples.title: Another practical example
